facts.fact: Name for the term: "Cơ quan đường bên"
Name for the term: "đường bên"
The lateral line is one of the fish's sense organs. It usually runs along the sides of the body.
The lateral line is made of cells and nerves in the skin. It matters to how a fish perceives its surroundings about as much as sight or hearing does.
Sense units called neuromasts sit on the body surface and in mucus-filled canals that run along the fish's sides.
Culum Brown (Macquarie University) says the lateral line makes a fish's whole outer body sensitive to vibrations in the water.
Fish use the lateral line to face into currents (rheotaxis), to school and to find prey, and some species use it to communicate.
Water flow and waves can disrupt what the lateral line senses.
Fish have no external ears. They sense vibrations through the lateral line and the otoliths ('ear stones').
Waves that bounce off aquarium walls could distress fish, because their lateral line is so sensitive.

Mary Power (UC Berkeley) suggests that reflections from tank walls could act like an echo chamber, 'like having constant loud noise'. She asks whether aggression or repetitive cleaning could come from an overstimulated lateral line.
John Montgomery (University of Auckland) says constant overstimulation is more likely to cause the lateral line to lose sensitivity than to cause acute discomfort.
Culum Brown suggests that keepers add structures such as logs and plants to break up the water movements that reflect off the tank walls.

Popular Science reports a 2019 study in which zebrafish preferred habitats with flowing water, possibly because flow lets them use their lateral lines. The article warns that this may not hold for every species.
Tapping on the glass sends vibrations through the water. These can be strong enough to panic fish, even when the tapping is on the far side of the tank.
A sudden noise can make fish flee and injure themselves on objects in the tank. The source says repeated stress raises cortisol and makes fish more likely to get sick.
Instead of tapping the glass to bring shy fish out, remove aggressive tankmates, add dense plants for cover, and tempt them with food.

A Vietnamese shop, AquaZone, says that small children tapping on the glass, or a net, can make fish dart and jump out of the tank. It advises keepers to watch for tapping and to avoid sudden handling near the tank.
Put the tank light on a timer and let the room light come on first, so the fish are not startled.
Head and lateral line erosion (HLLE), also called 'hole-in-the-head', is a serious condition that often affects fish kept in captivity.
HLLE starts as small lesions, usually on the head. They can spread along the lateral line and onto the unpaired fins.
Untreated HLLE lesions can grow into larger whitish pits, and the condition may be fatal.
HLLE looks like neuromastic pitting but is a different condition.
Seriously Fish says HLLE does not appear to occur in wild fish.

The cause of HLLE is not confirmed. It has been linked to protozoa of the genus Hexamita and to an autoimmune disorder, but neither link is proven. Poor water quality and poor nutrition make it worse.
Two studies link HLLE in closed marine aquarium systems to activated carbon. One of them names activated lignite carbon.
HLLE begins as small pits where the skin pulls back around the head and/or the lateral line. It is rarely fatal but leaves fish disfigured.
HLLE may be reversed with water changes of more than 90%. More often the fish are moved to a new aquarium that has never had a case of HLLE.
Fish shown or named on Wikipedia's HLLE page include the starry-night cichlid (Paratilapia polleni) and the severum (Heros).
Bệnh thủng đầu (hole-in-the-head) in cá dĩa (discus) usually starts as small holes on the head and the đường bên (lateral line).
Signs of hole-in-the-head in discus include small ulcers above the eyes and on both sides of the head, small holes around the lateral line, and stringy mucus on the skin and wounds.

Causes of hole-in-the-head in discus listed by a Vietnamese shop: long-term use of activated carbon, frequent feeding of beef heart and frozen bloodworms, lack of vitamins and minerals, the flagellate Spironucleus, Hexamita (disputed), and stress.

Cá Dĩa Đại Phát advises isolating the sick discus and treating with an anti-protozoal medicine such as Metronidazole, API General Cure, Fish Zole or Hikari Metro+, following the product's instructions.
Do not use pure RO or distilled water on its own. Mix it with tap water or add a mineral product such as Seachem Replenish.
Prevent hole-in-the-head with a varied diet rich in vitamins and minerals, little beef heart, and no activated carbon in the filter.
Hole-in-the-head shows as holes, pits or lesions on the head, face or lateral line. Severe cases have deep ulcers that bleed.

Aquarium Co-Op lists these causes of hole-in-the-head: Hexamita and Spironucleus multiplying when the fish's immunity is weak, new or feeder fish that carry disease, ammonia or nitrite above 0 ppm, the same food every day, and stress from bullying, cold or pH swings.

Treat with Fritz ParaCleanse (metronidazole and praziquantel). Remove activated carbon, keep aeration running, and follow the package's 5-day plan. Wait about 2 weeks, then repeat the 5-day course for parasite eggs that hatched.
If ParaCleanse does not help, Aquarium Co-Op suggests a copper-based medicine, starting at 1 drop per gallon to test the fish's tolerance. Copper can kill shrimp and snails.
Fast-growing live plants such as Pogostemon stellatus take up ammonia, nitrite and nitrate and help fish recover from hole-in-the-head.
If a fish does not improve, a fish vet can examine lesion scrapings, fecal samples and cultures. Recovery is not guaranteed.
Quarantine every new fish and do not share siphons or decorations between tanks. This helps keep hole-in-the-head out.
When hole-in-the-head is caught early, the holes close, but the new skin may stay discolored.
